chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
title: Lena Horne at the Sands and Sammy Davis's lean days
summary: Crawford tells of the pool being drained after Lena Horne's daughter swam in it and of Sammy Davis eating mustard sandwiches.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Bob was an unnecessarily cruel, big, imposing man. But he was a nice fellow. But he was always into trouble. And something else I want to say, that I remember time Lena Horne was working at the Sands, packing them in, Stanley, in Las Vegas. Lena put her young daughter, Keo, in the swimming pool at the Sands, left her in there, let her play around and swim.

Of course, naturally, she was going to be back and forth at the Sands. Now, she stayed at the Sands also, those big stars like that. Me -- I'll get to that. So -- no, I couldn't stay at the Sands. Stayed in a cottage across from the Sands or out somewhere. But Lena Horne put her daughter in the swimming pool, and do you know they drained all the water out of that pool --
-- you know, to get that colored -- little colored matter out of the pool, drained it out. And Lena's packing them in there.
And another thing, I remember being at the Sands with Sammy Davis.
Were you working with Lena Horne --

I made many records with her, George Duvinick DeVinney on bass and myself. And I was told by a friend of mine, Paul Quinichette, when he was staying with Sammy Davis here in New York in a hotel, any beat up hotels, and they used to eat ham and mustard sandwiches. And so when the ham ran out, Sammy and him ate mustard and bread sandwiches. Well, it was something to eat. It was better than I did in Cleveland.
And now look at Sammy Davis. He could afford any meal he wished. And that was another thing that -- shocking but just look at Sammy today. He can eat anything he want. So that was another experience.
